Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from what I have gathered. I was limited in searches and fetches, but I have substantial material from the main sources.

# Genesis 49 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## vv. 1–2: The Gathering for Prophecy

- **The first conscious prophecy spoken by a man in the Bible.** Earlier prophecies were announced by God directly (e.g., Genesis 3:15) or were veiled; here Jacob consciously speaks God's word over his sons as his last significant patriarchal act. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"In the last days"** (Hebrew *acharith hayyamim*, LXX *ep' eschaton tōn hēmerōn*): The phrase is an eschatological term. Keil and Delitzsch argue it means "not the future generally but the last future, the Messianic age of consummation." Others (e.g., amillennialist Utley, cited at Precept Austin) see it as relating to the conquest and settlement of Canaan. The King James Version Study Bible sees a dual perspective: occupation of Canaan *and* the coming of Messiah. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary
- **Jewish interpreters**, according to Nachmanides, understood "the last days" to mean the days of the Messiah. An ancient Jewish writing says Jacob wanted to reveal "the end of the Messiah" but was prevented. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/49.htm
- **"You sons of Jacob… listen to Israel your father"**: Jacob recognized he was both Jacob (what he battled against) and Israel (what God made him). This dual address signals spiritual maturity at the end of his life. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **The repetition** of "gather together" and "hear… listen" signals the weight and importance of what follows; each son's word was meant to be heard by all. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary

## vv. 3–4: Reuben — Instability and Loss of the Birthright

- **"My firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength"**: Reuben held the natural prerogatives of the firstborn — the excellency of dignity (chieftainship/priesthood) and excellency of power (ruling authority). Ellicott notes that as firstborn, these offices belonged to him by right. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"Unstable as water"** (or "boiling over like water"): The word is related to pride, wantonness, and lasciviousness. Ellicott notes the Arabic root means "boastful" and the Syriac "wantonness." The comparison with water well fits: water yields to every impression yet retains none. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"You shall not excel"**: Reuben forfeited the birthright through instability and the sin of sleeping with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22). The birthright was divided: the leadership went to Judah, the priesthood to Levi, and the double portion to Joseph. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **Historical fulfillment**: No prophet, judge, or king is known to have come from the tribe of Reuben. Ellicott confirms this: "As a matter of history no king, judge, or prophet is recorded as having sprung from the tribe of Reuben." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Spurgeon**: "So a man may have great opportunities, and yet lose them. Uncontrolled passions may make him very little who otherwise might have been great." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## vv. 5–7: Simeon and Levi — Fierce Anger and Scattering

- **"Simeon and Levi are brothers"**: They were alike not just in parentage but in disposition. They were close allies and likely tried to exercise tyrannical authority over younger brothers. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"Weapons of violence are their swords"** (or "their knives"): Ellicott argues the word for "habitations" is better translated "swords" or "knives." He suggests it may be the Greek word *machaera*, imported by Ionian traders. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **The sin remembered**: Their slaughter of the Shechemites (Genesis 34:25–29) in retaliation for Dinah's rape. Jacob did little at the time, but the sin carried consequences for generations. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce"**: The problem was not anger itself but that it was rooted in self-will. The difference between godly and ungodly anger is often self-will. Ellicott: "Jacob condemns Simeon and Levi not because they were angry, but because they vented their anger in a perfidious and violent manner." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"In their self-will they hamstrung an ox"** (or "houghed an ox"): Ellicott notes a possible double meaning — the literal hamstringing of oxen at Shechem, but also a figurative reference to disabling Joseph by selling him into slavery: "without any just cause for indignation, they hamstrung the noblest of their brethren, not killing Joseph outright, but disabling him by selling him into slavery." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **The scattering — a curse for Simeon, a blessing for Levi**: Simeon dwindled from 59,300 to 22,200 men in the wilderness (Numbers 1:23; 26:14) and was absorbed into Judah's territory. But Levi's scattering became a blessing when that tribe proved faithful at the golden calf (Exodus 32:26–28); the Lord became their inheritance instead of land (Joshua 13:33). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **Ellicott on the conditional nature**: "In Levi's case the curse was changed into a blessing by the faithfulness of the tribe upon a very trying occasion… we learn from it the great lesson that the Divine rewards and punishments, even when specified in prophecy, are nevertheless conditional upon human conduct." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Spurgeon**: "Happy is that man who, though he begins with a dark shadow resting upon him, so lives as to turn even that shadow into bright sunlight." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## vv. 8–12: Judah — The Royal Tribe and Messianic Promise

- **"Judah, your brothers shall praise you"**: The name Judah means "praise" (Genesis 29:35). Jacob now confirms it with a prophecy. Judah had sinned grievously (selling Joseph, the Tamar incident), but repented and offered himself as a substitute for Benjamin (Genesis 44:18–34), demonstrating selflessness. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **Judah inherits the firstborn's rights** because Reuben, Simeon, and Levi disqualified themselves. Ligonier/Reformed view: "Judah inherits the firstborn's rights because of his selflessness… Judah's repentance and exaltation illustrates the biblical principle that 'whoever humbles himself will be exalted' (Matt. 23:12)." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **"Your hand shall be on the necks of your enemies"**: Judah will triumph over his foes. Historically, Judah became Israel's chief tribe, the initial head after Joshua's death (Judges 1:1–2), and produced the Davidic dynasty. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **Spurgeon sees Judah as a type of Christ throughout**: "The dying patriarch was speaking of his own son Judah; but while speaking of Judah he had a special eye to our Lord, who sprang from the tribe of Judah. Everything therefore which he says of Judah, the type, he means with regard to our greater Judah, the antitype, our Lord Jesus Christ." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/ (citing Spurgeon). In his sermon "Praise for Jesus," Spurgeon says Jacob "seemed to forget his son and to turn his thoughts to Jesus, our Lord, of whom Judah was a very significant type." — https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons58/sermons58.xiv.html
- **"Judah is a lion's whelp… like a lioness"**: Ellicott notes Judah's chosen emblem was likely a lion. The imagery moves from a young lion (active, enterprising) to a full-grown lion (majestic in repose). The lioness is said to be fiercer than the male. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Matthew Henry** (cited by Ligonier): "Judah is compared, not to a lion rampant, always tearing, always raging, always ranging; but to a lion couchant, enjoying the satisfaction of his power and success, without creating vexation to others: this is to be truly great." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/messiahs-kingdom
- **"The scepter will not depart from Judah… until Shiloh comes"**: The central Messianic prophecy. A scepter is the symbol of royal command. Ellicott argues it indicates "tribal rather than royal rank" — that Judah would remain a "self-governed and legally-constituted tribe" until the appointed one comes. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html

### The Meaning of "Shiloh" — A Key Interpretive Debate

- **Traditional Messianic reading** ("Shiloh" as a proper name for Messiah): Enduring Word says the name means "He whose right it is" or "to Whom it belongs," understood anciently as the Messiah. The Targum of Onkelos paraphrases: "Until Messiah come, whose is the kingdom." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"Sheloh" = "whose it is"**: Ellicott argues the original reading was *Sheloh* (not *Shiloh*), an Aramaic form meaning "Whose it is." All ancient versions except the Vulgate read *Sheloh*. The LXX has "He for whom it is laid up." Ezekiel 21:27 quotes this using the Hebrew idiom "Until he come, whose is the right." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"Until tribute comes to him"**: The ESV translation (used by Ligonier). This rendering emphasizes the peoples' obedience and tribute to the coming king. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **NET Bible note** lists four major options: (1) Shiloh as a place name, (2) "until his ruler comes" (Davidic ruler/Messiah), (3) "until tribute is brought to him," (4) "to whom it belongs." All options point toward the Davidic monarchy or Messiah. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary
- **The historical argument for fulfillment**: From David until the Herods, a prince of Judah was head over Israel. Around AD 7, under Herod and the Romans, Israel's right to capital punishment — a last vestige of self-governance — was taken away. Rabbinic tradition records rabbis lamenting, "Woe unto us, for the scepter has been taken away from Judah, and Shiloh has not come." Yet Jesus was alive at that very time. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **Reformed view via John Calvin** (cited by Ligonier): "The kingdom which he [Jacob] transfers to the tribe of Judah, he declares shall be no common kingdom, because from it, at length, shall proceed the fullness of the promised benediction." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **"And the allegiance of the nations is his"**: Ellicott translates "obedience" rather than "gathering" (based on Proverbs 30:17, the only other OT use of the word). The Hebrew has "peoples" (plural) — not only Israel, but all nations. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Dr. Constable's Expository Notes**: Shiloh means "the bearer of rest," a proper name for Messiah. Everything after "until" describes millennial conditions. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-49.html (search result excerpt)

### v. 11: The Abundance Imagery

- **"He ties his donkey to the vine…"**: Ellicott sees this as hyperbole for the extraordinary fertility of Judah's land — vines so plentiful that a traveler would tie his donkey to one without concern. The "choice vine" (*sorek*) was a prized variety bearing small, luscious, seedless purple grapes. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Ligonier/Reformed reading**: "The abundance depicted in Genesis 49:11 proves Calvin's point. One of Judah's sons will rule over a kingdom so blessed that costly vines, the source of wine and income, will be hitches for donkeys. These animals would surely chew through such vines, but this is not a problem since the number of vines they own in the kingdom is so vast." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **Sailhamer** (cited by Constable): "Wine, the symbol of prosperity and blessing, will be so plentiful that even the choicest vines will be put to such everyday use as tethering the animals of burden and vintage wine will be as commonplace as wash water." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-49.html (search excerpt)

### v. 12: Eyes and Teeth

- **"His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk"**: Not describing Judah's personal appearance, but the prosperity of his descendants. Ellicott renders: "His eyes shall be brighter than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk" — a picture of health and abundance. The Vulgate renders "beautiful." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html

## v. 13: Zebulun — Dwelling by the Sea

- **Zebulun's territory** lay between the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean, but did not actually reach the Mediterranean shore. Ellicott notes this: his land was near the inland sea of Gennesaret. The prophecy may indicate that Zebulun would be a tribe of traders rather than agriculturists, interacting with the Phoenicians. Moses also speaks of Zebulun "sucking of the abundance of the seas." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Enduring Word**: "Literally, 'shall dwell by the haven of the sea' can be translated 'looking towards the sea.' Zebulun did look to the sea, both to the east and west." They were noted for supplying the largest number of soldiers to David's army (1 Chronicles 12:33). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## vv. 14–15: Issachar — The Strong Donkey in Servitude

- **"A strong donkey"**: Ellicott says this comes from Issachar's chosen signet emblem (the ass — in the East, a noble, spirited, enduring animal). But his real character was "slothful, inactive, and commonplace." "Strong ass" (Hebrew: "an ass of bone") means coarsely bred — animals of high parentage have small bones. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"Lying down between the sheepfolds"**: The dual-form word refers to the two-part pens used for larger and smaller cattle. The image is of a tribe "stretched at ease between his cattle-pens… occupied with pastoral pursuits, and destitute of all higher aspirations." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"He bent his shoulder to the burden"**: Ellicott explains "a servant unto tribute" (Hebrew: *task-work*) means forced labor — the kind Solomon exacted from Canaanites (1 Kings 9:21). Issachar would accept injustice because their land was prosperous. Enduring Word (citing Leupold): "Issachar was strong, but docile and lazy. He would enjoy the good land assigned him but would not strive for it. Therefore, eventually he would be pressed into servitude." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## vv. 16–18: Dan — Justice, Serpent, and the Cry for Salvation

- **"Dan shall provide justice for his people"**: A wordplay on the name Dan ("judge"). Ellicott: Jacob assured the sons of the handmaids they would have independent tribal status. Dan would "judge his people as a distinct and separate tribe, possessed of all those rights of self-government and tribal independence which this rank implied." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **"A snake by the road, a viper in the path"**: Dan's emblem was likely a serpent. The "arrow-snake" lies in wait in a narrow track and springs upon its prey. Though too weak to take the foremost place in war, Dan would not be without military importance — notably in the days of Samson (Judges 13:2). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Dan's idolatry**: The tribe introduced idolatry into Israel (Judges 18:30). Jeroboam set up a golden calf in Dan (1 Kings 12:26–30), and later Dan was a center of idol worship (Amos 8:14). Some think the serpent imagery points to the antichrist coming from Dan (based on Daniel 11:37 and Jeremiah 8:16). Dan is omitted from the 144,000 in Revelation 7 but is first in Ezekiel's millennial roll call (Ezekiel 48), a sign of redemption. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"I await Your salvation, O LORD"** (v. 18): The Hebrew for "salvation" is *yeshuwah*. Jacob, near death, cried out for God's salvation. Ellicott suggests the thought of the serpent wounding the prey's heel carried Jacob's mind back to Genesis 3:15 — the fall of man and the promise of the Deliverer. "Thus it is a profession of faith… in the advent in due time of the promised Deliverer." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html
- **Spurgeon**: "What a happy breathing-space is this! When you and I also are near our journey's end, may we be able to say, as Jacob did, 'I have waited for thy salvation, O Lord.'" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics suggests this exclamation was intended to form "a kind of middle point, separating the groups of blessings into one of seven, and another of five." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/genesis/49.htm

## v. 19: Gad — Attacked but Triumphant

- **"Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will attack their heels"**: A wordplay on Gad (from *gadad*, "to gather in troops"). Ellicott: "A troop of plunderers shall throng upon him, but he shall throng upon their heel." The tribe of Gad supplied many fine troops for David (1 Chronicles 12:14). In the days of Jeremiah, foreign armies oppressed Gad (Jeremiah 49:1), yet victory would be theirs. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-49.html (partial — content cut off in fetch)
- **Spurgeon**: "This has been the blessing of many a child of God – to fight, and apparently to lose the battle, yet to win it at the end." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## v. 20: Asher — Royal Delicacies

- **"Asher's food will be rich; he shall provide royal delicacies"**: The land allotted to Asher was exceptionally fertile. Moses later said: "Asher is most blessed of sons; let him be favored by his brothers, and let him dip his foot in oil" (Deuteronomy 33:24). The region produced not only necessities but luxuries fit for kings. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## v. 21: Naphtali — A Doe Set Free

- **"Naphtali is a doe set free that bears beautiful fawns"** (or "he uses beautiful words"): Naphtali's territory was near the Sea of Galilee, the region where Jesus did much of His teaching and ministry (Matthew 4:12–16 — "the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali"). Because so much of Jesus' ministry took place there, Enduring Word notes that the prophecy of "beautiful words" was fittingly spoken of this tribe. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## vv. 22–26: Joseph — The Fruitful Vine and the Abundant Blessing

- **"Joseph is a fruitful vine"** (or "fruitful bough"): The image is of a vine well-watered, "by a spring," with branches running over the wall. This speaks of Joseph's deep relationship with God. Enduring Word cites Spurgeon: "The main point in Joseph's character was that he was in clear and constant fellowship with God, and therefore God blessed him greatly." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"The archers attacked him with bitterness"**: Joseph was "shot at and hated" — by his brothers, by Potiphar's wife, by forgetful fellow-prisoners — yet he remained fruitful. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"His strong arms were tempered by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob"**: God's hands were on Joseph's hands, giving him strength and skill. God was present even when Joseph did not know it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **Five titles for God** in this passage: "The Mighty One of Jacob," "the Shepherd," "the Rock of Israel," "the God of your father," and "the Almighty" (*Shaddai*). Enduring Word notes this shows Jacob had come to a profound personal knowledge of God — far better than earlier when he called God "the Fear of his father Isaac" (Genesis 31:53). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"Blessings of the breasts and womb"**: Fertility blessings — fruitfulness in family and livestock. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"The blessings of your father have surpassed the blessings of the ancient mountains"**: Jacob could say this because he knew how much God had forgiven him. He was forgiven much and loved much (Luke 7:47). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"The prince of his brothers"**: Joseph was "separate from his brothers" (*nazir*) — set apart by his suffering and his character. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## v. 27: Benjamin — The Ravenous Wolf

- **"Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he devours the prey, in the evening he divides the plunder"**: This tribe had a reputation for fierceness. Examples: Ehud the judge (Judges 3:15–23), King Saul (1 Samuel 9:1, 14:47–52), and the apostle Paul before his conversion (Acts 8:1–3). The cruelty of the tribe is seen in Judges 19–20. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## v. 28: The Twelve Tribes Blessed

- **"He blessed them; he blessed each one with a suitable blessing"**: Some of the words were harsh, but even the rebukes were part of God's prophetic word about each tribe's destiny. Each tribe had its own calling. The remarkable promise was that they would survive and grow into significant tribes despite centuries in Egypt. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## vv. 29–32: Jacob's Burial Instructions

- **"I am about to be gathered to my people"**: Jacob was confident that Abraham and Isaac continued to live in the eternal state and that he would join them. Enduring Word: "Jacob was confident that his father Isaac and his grandfather Abraham continued to live in the eternal state." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **"Bury me with my fathers"**: Though in Egypt and honored enough to be buried like a Pharaoh, Jacob chose an obscure cave in Canaan because Canaan was the land promised by covenant. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **The cave of Machpelah**: Abraham had purchased it from Ephron the Hittite (Genesis 23). Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah were buried there; Jacob had buried Leah there. The purchase from the Hittites established legal ownership, underscoring the legitimacy of the patriarchal claim to the land. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

## v. 33: The Death of Jacob

- **"He pulled his feet into the bed and breathed his last, and he was gathered to his people"**: Jacob did not die until he had finished delivering every word God had given him. Enduring Word cites a remark: "Jacob did not yield up the ghost until he had delivered the last sentence of admonition and benediction to his twelve sons. He was immortal till his work was done." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/

---

## Points of Distinctive Interpretation Across Traditions

### The Shiloh Prophecy (v. 10)

- **Reformed (Ligonier/Calvin)**: Emphasis on the Davidic monarchy as fulfillment and on Judah inheriting the firstborn's rights through repentance. Calvin: "The kingdom which he transfers to the tribe of Judah… shall be no common kingdom." The kingdom described in v. 11 points to the Messiah's kingdom of abundance. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/judahs-scepter
- **Baptist (Spurgeon)**: Strongly Christological and typological. Judah is almost entirely eclipsed by Christ. Spurgeon treats the whole passage as directly about Jesus: Judah's praise, his hand on his enemies' necks, his lion-like power, his perpetual sovereignty — all find their ultimate meaning in Christ. — https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons58/sermons58.xiv.html
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik)**: Combines historical fulfillment with Messianic application. Notes the rabbinic tradition about the scepter departing in AD 7 and Jesus being alive at that very moment. Emphasizes that the prophecy took 640 years for partial fulfillment (David) and 1,600 for complete fulfillment (Jesus). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-49/
- **Evangelical (Precept Austin)**: Cites multiple evangelical sources (MacArthur, Ryrie, Keil & Delitzsch, Morris). Affirms the Messianic interpretation while noting the debate: amillennial interpreters (Utley) see it as relating to the conquest, while dispensationalists see eschatological implications reaching to the Second Coming. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary

### The "Last Days" (v. 1)

- **Amillennial view (Utley, cited at Precept Austin)**: The time frame relates to the conquest and settlement of Canaan, possibly extending to the early monarchy; it does not fit an end-times framework. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary
- **Dispensational/Premillennial view**: The phrase is genuinely eschatological, pointing to events just before Messiah's Second Coming, noting Revelation 7's listing of the twelve tribes. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary
- **Reformed/Covenant view (Reformation Study Bible, cited at Precept Austin)**: "Jacob's prophecies embrace the entire history of Israel from the conquest and distribution of the land to the reign of the Messiah, Jesus Christ." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-49-commentary

### Levi's Scattering (v. 7)

- **All surveyed traditions agree** that what was a curse for Simeon became a blessing for Levi when they stood faithful at the golden calf (Exodus 32). The difference lies in emphasis: Enduring Word highlights this as a principle of suffering transformed into blessing; Ellicott emphasizes the conditional nature of prophecy.

## What Could Not Be Found

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings**: Searches to newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not return usable results within the search/fetch limits. These views are not represented in the notes above.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan/Holiness sources**: No results from wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed.com were retrieved within the limits.
- **Lutheran sources**: No results from lcms.org or 1517.org were retrieved.
- **Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org)**: The NET Bible note on Shiloh was cited secondarily through Precept Austin but could not be fetched directly.
- **Desiring God (John Piper) or GTY (John MacArthur)**: MacArthur's note on "the last days" appears in the Precept Austin compilation, but no dedicated sermon or article was fetched from these sites.
